screens.title: Generics for Reusable Code Structures
screens.narratorSegment: Today we explore generics in C#, a tool that helps you avoid repeated code while preserving compile-time type safety. Generics let you write a single class or method with a placeholder type, conventionally called T, and then supply concrete types when you use that code. This matters in game development where you often repeat similar systems for enemies, projectiles, and effects. For example, instead of creating three separate pools for bullets, enemies, and particles, you can build a single ObjectPool that recycles any Component-derived object. You will see how a constraint like where T : Component allows the pool to call Instantiate and access gameObject safely. We will also cover generic methods and generic constraints, common pitfalls like using object or missing constraints, and a hands-on Singleton pattern to reduce repetition for manager classes. By the end, you'll understand when to reach for generics, how to apply constraints correctly, and how these patterns improve maintainability and runtime performance in Unity projects. Consider one system in your current project where a single generic type could replace duplicated logic.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These learning objectives frame the practical skills you'll build with generics in C# for Unity. First, you will understand the concept of generics and why a type parameter acts as a placeholder that the compiler checks for correctness. Second, you'll implement generic classes that let a single implementation serve many types, which reduces duplicate code and makes maintenance easier. Third, you will learn to implement generic methods so utility functions can accept any appropriate type parameter. Finally on this screen you'll see how generic constraints limit which types can be used, enabling safe calls to Unity APIs. Each objective ties directly to common game-development tasks: collections, pooling, and manager patterns. As you work through the examples and code walkthroughs, focus on the rule that constraints tell the compiler what members you can safely access. If you bypass generics with object or unchecked casts, you lose compile-time guarantees and invite runtime errors. Keep these objectives in mind as your plan for applying generics to concrete systems in your projects.

screens.title: What are generics in C#?
screens.narratorSegment: Generics let you write classes, interfaces, and methods that defer the choice of one or more types until the code is used. Instead of fixing a concrete type inside the implementation, you declare a type parameter, conventionally named T, that acts as a placeholder. A familiar example is List. The List class manages storage and resizing logic once, while T becomes the specific type you need at each use site — List<Enemy> or List<PowerUp>. This preserves compile-time type safety: the compiler enforces that only items of the chosen type are added to the collection. An important consequence is fewer casts and earlier detection of type mismatches. A common misconception is thinking generics are only collections — they apply equally to utility classes, pools, and patterns like singletons. For example, a generic Stack<T> can be used for ints, strings, or InventoryItem objects with the same push and pop logic. Takeaway: generics separate what a structure does from which concrete type it acts on, letting you write one correct implementation and reuse it safely across many types. Ask yourself where repeated, type-specific code in your project could become a single generic blueprint.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: A generic defers the concrete type until use by introducing a type parameter, enabling one implementation to serve many types with compile-time safety.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › What are generics in C#?
Generics — the concept
A type parameter lets one blueprint work with many concrete types while keeping compile-time checks.
Why this matters
  • Reduces repeated code across types like Enemy, Projectile, PowerUp.
  • Lets the compiler check types instead of relying on casts.
  • Applies to classes, interfaces, and methods beyond collections.
Concrete analogy
Think of a single mold where T selects the material — same mold, different outputs.
Code example — List<T>
// Usage, not implementation
List<Enemy> enemies = new List<Enemy>();
enemies.Add(new Enemy());
Enemy first = enemies[0];

// Same generic list for different types
List<PowerUp> powerUps = new List<PowerUp>();
Common misconception
Generics are not only for collections. Any reusable structure or pattern can be generic.
Key Takeaway

Use generics to separate behavior from concrete types and let the compiler enforce correct usage.

screens.title: Understanding the type parameter T
screens.narratorSegment: The type parameter, often named T, is at the heart of generics. It is a placeholder inside a generic definition that is replaced by a concrete type when the code is instantiated. For example, when you declare List<Enemy>, the compiler substitutes Enemy for T and enforces that only Enemy instances are stored in that list. This substitution gives you compile-time guarantees: you cannot accidentally add a PowerUp to a List<Enemy> without a cast, and you avoid runtime type failures. Type parameters can be used anywhere a regular type is used—fields, method parameters, return types—making the generic type behave like a strongly typed container or service. A subtle point is that generics preserve the operations available on a type only when constraints allow them; without a constraint the compiler only treats T as an object with no special members. Misconception to avoid: type parameters do not create new runtime types for each T; they produce type-safe constructs that the compiler validates. Ask yourself what operations your generic needs to perform and use constraints when those operations require specific members. Understanding the type parameter T means t is a placeholder replaced by a concrete type at instantiation; the compiler enforces that usage matches that concrete type.. In practical terms, how t becomes a concrete type and what the compiler enforces. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Type Parameter
What T means in practice
When you pick T, the compiler enforces type rules for that usage. This reduces casts and errors.
Example substitution
// The placeholder T becomes Enemy here
List<Enemy> enemies = new List<Enemy>();
enemies.Add(new Enemy());
Enemy e = enemies[0];
What the compiler guarantees
  • Only the chosen type can be added without casts.
  • Methods and properties typed with T return the concrete type.
  • Type safety happens at compile time, catching many bugs early.
Misconception check
Generics are not dynamic typing. They are compile-time constructs that enforce static types, not runtime polymorphism on arbitrary members.
When to add constraints
If your code needs to call members that not all types have, use a constraint so the compiler knows those members exist. The next lesson covers constraints with Unity examples.
Key Takeaway

Pick T to generalize behavior and add constraints when you need guaranteed members on T.

keyIdea.title: Stack<T>
keyIdea.text: A single generic stack implementation can hold any concrete type while preserving compile-time safety for push and pop operations.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Designing a generic Stack<T>
Stack<T> — code walkthrough
One implementation, many types—useful for command histories or transient buffers.
public class Stack<T>
{
  private List<T> _items = new List<T>();

  public void Push(T item)
  {
    _items.Add(item);
  }

  public T Pop()
  {
    if (_items.Count == 0)
      throw new InvalidOperationException("Stack is empty.");
    T item = _items[_items.Count - 1];
    _items.RemoveAt(_items.Count - 1);
    return item;
  }

  public T Peek()
  {
    if (_items.Count == 0)
      throw new InvalidOperationException("Stack is empty.");
    return _items[_items.Count - 1];
  }

  public int Count => _items.Count;
}
Usage example
Use Stack<int> for counters or Stack<InventoryItem> for item undo operations without rewriting stack logic.
Why this pattern helps
  • Single tested implementation works for any type T.
  • Compile-time checks prevent incorrect item types being pushed or popped.
  • Eliminates repetitive stacks like IntStack, StringStack, or ItemStack.
Common mistake
Using object and casting defeats the safety and clarity generics provide. Prefer Stack<T> over object-based containers.
Key Takeaway

Generic collections let you reuse robust algorithms while keeping the compiler as an ally for correctness.

screens.title: Why and how to use generic constraints
screens.narratorSegment: Generic constraints specify the requirements a type argument must meet, allowing the compiler to know which members exist on T. In Unity, a common constraint is where T : Component, which guarantees that T has a gameObject property and can be instantiated by Object. Instantiate. Without that constraint the compiler treats T as an object with no Unity-specific members available. Constraints can require interfaces, base classes, constructors, or the class/struct nature of the type, for example where T : MonoBehaviour or where T : new(). A concrete example from the chapter is ObjectPool<T> where T : Component. Because of that clause, the pool can call Object. Instantiate(_prefab, _parent) and use obj. gameObject. SetActive(false) safely. A common misconception is that constraints restrict generic usefulness; in fact they enable useful operations safely. Use constraints only when your generic implementation needs the members or behavior they guarantee. When you see compiler errors about unknown members on T, that is a signal you likely need an appropriate where clause. Why and how to use generic constraints means constraints inform the compiler what members or behaviors a type parameter must provide, enabling safe calls on t inside generic code.. In practical terms, using where clauses to enable safe operations on t. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Generic Constraints
What constraints do
They tell the compiler what operations on T are valid inside the generic code.
// Example constraint used in the chapter
public class ObjectPool<T> where T : Component
{
  // Pool implementation that can call obj.gameObject
}
Common constraint forms
  • where T : Component or MonoBehaviour
  • where T : class or where T : struct
  • where T : new() for requiring a parameterless constructor
Misconception check
Constraints don't reduce flexibility when you need specific members; they increase safety by documenting and enforcing requirements.
Why this matters in Unity
A Component constraint ensures you can call Instantiate, access gameObject, and use Unity lifecycle members without casting.
Key Takeaway

Add constraints when your generic needs guaranteed members; they let you call Unity API safely inside generic code.

screens.title: Object pooling pattern in game development
screens.narratorSegment: Object pooling is a design pattern that pre-instantiates a set of objects and reuses them instead of frequently creating and destroying GameObjects. In games, frequent instantiation can cause garbage collection spikes and dropped frames, especially for bullets, particles, or short-lived enemies. A pool keeps inactive objects ready and toggles them active when needed, then returns them to the pool when no longer in use. The generic ObjectPool<T> takes this pattern further: write the logic once and reuse it for different Component-derived types by supplying the prefab's component as T. The pattern includes initialization, get, return, and clear operations. A common mistake is to grow the pool without bounds; prefer controlled expansion or warnings when empty, as shown in the example that logs when the pool is expanded. Consider: if your game has many transient objects created per frame, an object pool can dramatically reduce allocations and keep your frame times stable. The next lesson shows the concrete ObjectPool<T> code from the chapter. Object pooling pattern in game development means pool objects to recycle instances, reduce allocations, and avoid frequent instantiate/destroy cycles that can hurt frame times.. In practical terms, why pools matter and when to use them. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Object Pooling
keyIdea.text: Pool objects to recycle instances, reduce allocations, and avoid frequent Instantiate/Destroy cycles that can hurt frame times.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Object pooling pattern
Why pools reduce costs
Pooling avoids repeated allocation and deallocation of GameObjects during gameplay, which helps maintain steady frame rates.
Core operations
  • Initialize: create a limited set of inactive objects.
  • Get: activate and return an object.
  • Return: deactivate and enqueue for reuse.
  • Clear: destroy pooled objects when necessary.
Design considerations
Decide initial size, whether to expand, and how to handle dependencies that must be reset on reuse.
Practical scenario

A shooter that spawns dozens of bullets per second benefits from pooled projectiles to avoid spikes from create/destroy cycles.

Key Takeaway

Pool short-lived, frequently created objects to lower runtime allocations and improve frame stability.

Common mistake
Filling pools without reset logic can leak state across uses. Always reset object state on Get or in Initialize.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Implementing ObjectPool<T>
ObjectPool<T> (key parts)
using System.Collections.Generic;
using UnityEngine;

public class ObjectPool<T> where T : Component
{
  private readonly Queue<T> _pool = new Queue<T>();
  private readonly T _prefab;
  private readonly Transform _parent;
  private readonly int _initialSize;

  public ObjectPool(T prefab, Transform parent, int initialSize)
  {
    _prefab = prefab;
    _parent = parent;
    _initialSize = initialSize;
    InitializePool();
  }

  private void InitializePool()
  {
    for (int i = 0; i < _initialSize; i++)
    {
      T obj = Object.Instantiate(_prefab, _parent);
      obj.gameObject.SetActive(false);
      _pool.Enqueue(obj);
    }
  }

  public T Get()
  {
    if (_pool.Count == 0)
    {
      Debug.LogWarning($"Pool for {_prefab.name} is empty. Expanding pool.");
      T newObj = Object.Instantiate(_prefab, _parent);
      newObj.gameObject.SetActive(false);
      _pool.Enqueue(newObj);
    }

    T objToGet = _pool.Dequeue();
    objToGet.gameObject.SetActive(true);
    return objToGet;
  }

  public void Return(T obj)
  {
    obj.gameObject.SetActive(false);
    _pool.Enqueue(obj);
  }

  public void Clear()
  {
    foreach (T obj in _pool)
    {
      if (obj != null)
      {
        Object.Destroy(obj.gameObject);
      }
    }
    _pool.Clear();
  }
}
Mapping methods to operations
  • InitializePool: creates inactive objects and enqueues them.
  • Get: ensures at least one object exists, activates, and returns it.
  • Return: deactivates and enqueues for later reuse.
  • Clear: destroys pooled objects and clears the queue.
Practical tip
Reset any runtime state on Get to avoid leaking state between usages, for example position, velocity, or timers.
Key Takeaway

The where clause is essential: it makes Unity-specific calls safe inside the generic pool code.

Spawner example
public class ProjectileSpawner : MonoBehaviour
{
  public GameObject projectilePrefab; // assign a prefab that has a Projectile component
  private ObjectPool<Projectile> _projectilePool;

  void Awake()
  {
    Projectile prefabComponent = projectilePrefab.GetComponent<Projectile>();
    if (prefabComponent == null)
    {
      Debug.LogError("Projectile prefab must have a Projectile component!");
      return;
    }
    _projectilePool = new ObjectPool<Projectile>(prefabComponent, transform, 10);
  }

  public void SpawnProjectile(Vector3 position, Quaternion rotation)
  {
    Projectile projectile = _projectilePool.Get();
    projectile.transform.position = position;
    projectile.transform.rotation = rotation;
    projectile.Initialize();
  }

  public void ReturnProjectile(Projectile projectile)
  {
    _projectilePool.Return(projectile);
  }
}
Important runtime details
  • Verify the prefab contains the required component before creating the pool.
  • Initialize object state after Get to ensure consistent behavior.
  • Return objects instead of Destroy to maintain the pool's benefits.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Singleton<T> activity
Singleton<T> template
using UnityEngine;

public class Singleton<T> : MonoBehaviour where T : MonoBehaviour
{
  private static T _instance;
  private static readonly object _lock = new object();
  private static bool _applicationIsQuitting = false;

  public static T Instance
  {
    get
    {
      if (_applicationIsQuitting)
      {
        Debug.LogWarning($"[Singleton] Instance '{typeof(T)}' already destroyed on application quit. Won't create again - returning null.");
        return null;
      }

      lock (_lock)
      {
        if (_instance == null)
        {
          _instance = (T)FindObjectOfType(typeof(T));

          if (FindObjectsOfType(typeof(T)).Length > 1)
          {
            Debug.LogError("[Singleton] Something went terribly wrong - there should never be more than 1 singleton!");
            return _instance;
          }

          if (_instance == null)
          {
            GameObject singleton = new GameObject();
            _instance = singleton.AddComponent<T>();
            singleton.name = "(Singleton) " + typeof(T).ToString();

            DontDestroyOnLoad(singleton);

            Debug.Log("[Singleton] An instance of " + typeof(T) + " was created with DontDestroyOnLoad.");
          }
        }
        return _instance;
      }
    }
  }

  public void OnDestroy()
  {
    _applicationIsQuitting = true;
  }
}
Practical notes
  • Use this for managers that must be globally accessible.
  • Be cautious: singletons can hide cross-component dependencies if overused.
  • Test across scene loads to confirm the instance persists as expected.
Key Takeaway

A generic Singleton<T> reduces boilerplate, letting you reuse a single, well-tested pattern for multiple manager types.

Assessment target
Create a Stack<T> that enforces type safety and has clear error behavior.
public class Stack<T>
{
  private List<T> _items = new List<T>();
  public void Push(T item) => _items.Add(item);

  public T Pop()
  {
    if (_items.Count == 0)
      throw new InvalidOperationException("Stack is empty.");
    T item = _items[_items.Count - 1];
    _items.RemoveAt(_items.Count - 1);
    return item;
  }

  public T Peek() { /* similar check then return last */ }
  public int Count => _items.Count;
}

  • Type-safe methods that accept and return T
  • Proper error handling for empty stack operations

Returning default(T) hides errors; prefer explicit exceptions so callers handle empty conditions appropriately.

fullNarratorScript:
Today we explore generics in C#, a tool that helps you avoid repeated code while preserving compile-time type safety. Generics let you write a single class or method with a placeholder type, conventionally called T, and then supply concrete types when you use that code. This matters in game development where you often repeat similar systems for enemies, projectiles, and effects. For example, instead of creating three separate pools for bullets, enemies, and particles, you can build a single ObjectPool that recycles any Component-derived object. You will see how a constraint like where T : Component allows the pool to call Instantiate and access gameObject safely. We will also cover generic methods and generic constraints, common pitfalls like using object or missing constraints, and a hands-on Singleton pattern to reduce repetition for manager classes. By the end, you'll understand when to reach for generics, how to apply constraints correctly, and how these patterns improve maintainability and runtime performance in Unity projects. Consider one system in your current project where a single generic type could replace duplicated logic.

These learning objectives frame the practical skills you'll build with generics in C# for Unity. First, you will understand the concept of generics and why a type parameter acts as a placeholder that the compiler checks for correctness. Second, you'll implement generic classes that let a single implementation serve many types, which reduces duplicate code and makes maintenance easier. Third, you will learn to implement generic methods so utility functions can accept any appropriate type parameter. Finally on this screen you'll see how generic constraints limit which types can be used, enabling safe calls to Unity APIs. Each objective ties directly to common game-development tasks: collections, pooling, and manager patterns. As you work through the examples and code walkthroughs, focus on the rule that constraints tell the compiler what members you can safely access. If you bypass generics with object or unchecked casts, you lose compile-time guarantees and invite runtime errors. Keep these objectives in mind as your plan for applying generics to concrete systems in your projects.

This second objectives screen focuses on applied skills you'll practice. Generics let you write classes, interfaces, and methods that defer the choice of one or more types until the code is used. Instead of fixing a concrete type inside the implementation, you declare a type parameter, conventionally named T, that acts as a placeholder. A familiar example is List. The List class manages storage and resizing logic once, while T becomes the specific type you need at each use site — List<Enemy> or List<PowerUp>. This preserves compile-time type safety: the compiler enforces that only items of the chosen type are added to the collection. An important consequence is fewer casts and earlier detection of type mismatches. A common misconception is thinking generics are only collections — they apply equally to utility classes, pools, and patterns like singletons. For example, a generic Stack<T> can be used for ints, strings, or InventoryItem objects with the same push and pop logic. Takeaway: generics separate what a structure does from which concrete type it acts on, letting you write one correct implementation and reuse it safely across many types. Ask yourself where repeated, type-specific code in your project could become a single generic blueprint.

The type parameter, often named T, is at the heart of generics. It is a placeholder inside a generic definition that is replaced by a concrete type when the code is instantiated. For example, when you declare List<Enemy>, the compiler substitutes Enemy for T and enforces that only Enemy instances are stored in that list. This substitution gives you compile-time guarantees: you cannot accidentally add a PowerUp to a List<Enemy> without a cast, and you avoid runtime type failures. Type parameters can be used anywhere a regular type is used—fields, method parameters, return types—making the generic type behave like a strongly typed container or service. A subtle point is that generics preserve the operations available on a type only when constraints allow them; without a constraint the compiler only treats T as an object with no special members. Misconception to avoid: type parameters do not create new runtime types for each T; they produce type-safe constructs that the compiler validates. Ask yourself what operations your generic needs to perform and use constraints when those operations require specific members. Generic constraints specify the requirements a type argument must meet, allowing the compiler to know which members exist on T. In Unity, a common constraint is where T : Component, which guarantees that T has a gameObject property and can be instantiated by Object. Instantiate. Without that constraint the compiler treats T as an object with no Unity-specific members available. Constraints can require interfaces, base classes, constructors, or the class/struct nature of the type, for example where T : MonoBehaviour or where T : new(). A concrete example from the chapter is ObjectPool<T> where T : Component. Because of that clause, the pool can call Object. Instantiate(_prefab, _parent) and use obj. gameObject. SetActive(false) safely. A common misconception is that constraints restrict generic usefulness; in fact they enable useful operations safely. Use constraints only when your generic implementation needs the members or behavior they guarantee. When you see compiler errors about unknown members on T, that is a signal you likely need an appropriate where clause. Object pooling is a design pattern that pre-instantiates a set of objects and reuses them instead of frequently creating and destroying GameObjects. In games, frequent instantiation can cause garbage collection spikes and dropped frames, especially for bullets, particles, or short-lived enemies. A pool keeps inactive objects ready and toggles them active when needed, then returns them to the pool when no longer in use. The generic ObjectPool<T> takes this pattern further: write the logic once and reuse it for different Component-derived types by supplying the prefab's component as T. The pattern includes initialization, get, return, and clear operations. A common mistake is to grow the pool without bounds; prefer controlled expansion or warnings when empty, as shown in the example that logs when the pool is expanded. Consider: if your game has many transient objects created per frame, an object pool can dramatically reduce allocations and keep your frame times stable. Generics are powerful, but they are sometimes misused or misapplied. Two common mistakes are using object instead of generics, and omitting necessary constraints. Using object forces callers to cast and defers type checks to runtime, which sacrifices both safety and performance. Omitting constraints prevents the compiler from knowing which members exist on T, so calls like obj. gameObject will cause errors; the solution is to add a where T : Component or appropriate interface. Another mistake is over-generalizing: for one-off functions that never repeat, a generic abstraction may add unnecessary complexity. Contrast this with proper use: a Stack<T> or ObjectPool<T> replaces many duplicated classes while preserving type-specific behavior. When you design a generic, ask: does the operation need members only some types provide? If yes, add constraints. If not, and the generic would be used in many places, it is likely the right abstraction. The takeaway is to balance generality with clarity and enforce constraints to keep code both flexible and safe. Generics provide three practical benefits for game development: maintainability, flexibility, and performance. Maintainability improves because you write logic once and reuse it; for example a single ObjectPool<T> replaces separate pool classes for each object type, reducing duplicated bugs and easing updates. Flexibility comes from being able to supply different concrete types without changing the implementation — List<Enemy> and List<PowerUp> share the same code. Performance benefits arise indirectly: using a pool reduces allocations and garbage collection work, keeping frame times steadier. Generics also reduce runtime casting overhead by using compile-time checks. However, remember that generics are a tool, not a hammer — they are most effective when a clear repeated pattern exists. When types require specific members, use constraints to enable safe operations. In short, when you spot repeated type-specific code, consider a generic solution to simplify maintenance and reduce runtime surprises.
